prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as a single part, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1; what has changed is that I now think the citation wording matters more than I first allowed. The scientific core is intact: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid interrogating many trapped atoms, and the statistical power of many atoms is what makes 1e-18 reachable. Ye's group then carried the clock to the systematic frontier and into many-body-aware operation. Independent reproduction in Sr and Yb at several national laboratories is as strong as for anything on the shortlist. The chair asks for a delivered fundamental-physics result and not only prospective use. From recollection, which I have not verified here, the best examples are the resolution of the gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale height differences within a single sample, and clock-comparison bounds on drifts of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings. Those are results that no earlier clock could deliver, so I do not think the case rests on promise alone. On the chair's wording question, I would tie the citation to the invention and its realisation at 1e-18 and say nothing about who was first to a given number, because several laboratories share the 1e-18 milestones and a record can be superseded. That wording credits the concept to Katori and the performance frontier to Ye, and it leaves the comb and ion-clock lineage, and the Sr, Yb and Hg groups, outside the claim.
statement.case_against: The reservations I listed in round 1 stand and I do not think round 2 has dissolved them. B009 follows the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems), and a sceptic can say that atomic precision measurement has been served three times in twenty years. Eight members ranking it, and now all eight preferring it, partly reflects movement after the openings, as the chair observes, and Danielsson is right that breadth of agreement is not depth of scientific weight. Some of the strongest consequences, especially a redefinition of the second and clock-based searches for new physics, are still prospective; the delivered results I can cite are tests, not discoveries of new physics. Credit is also genuinely narrower than the history: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, Gill and the PTB and NIST groups contributed decisive milestones and are outside any two-name prize. I accept those costs because the concept is separable and original and because the alternatives each carry a larger unresolved problem of their own.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B009 from fifth to his preferred configuration but warns that broad support is the safe consensus pick, that the clock is a metrology invention sitting uneasily with a discovery criterion after 2005 and 2012, and that clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own; he also asks that my Hall-laboratory tie be noted when B009 is discussed.
responses.response: I take the warning about consensus seriously and I do not want my own first place counted as independent weight. I would answer the criterion question in two parts. First, the founding act is an invention, and the Nobel will is explicit that it covers inventions as well as discoveries, so category alone should not decide it. Second, I partly concede the delivered-result point: clock comparisons have so far set bounds on constants and dark-matter couplings and resolved the redshift on millimetre scales, which is closer to measurement of a known effect at unprecedented precision than to a new phenomenon. If the committee reads the criterion as requiring a new phenomenon, B018 is the better answer and I would say so in my ballot. I also agree the Hall tie should be recorded when B009 is discussed, and I address it in my conflict note.

responses.point: Eriksson says B009 would drop for him if the committee decides the prize should reward a change in what physicists can think about rather than in what they can measure, and he asks that the citation be written around the invention and its realisation and not around a record number that may be superseded.
responses.response: I accept his citation point and have changed my wording accordingly: the 1e-18 level now appears as the level at which the invention was realised, not as a record. On his conditional, I think the measurement-versus-thinking distinction is real, but I would resist treating it as a binary test. The clock changes what can be thought about in a modest way, because many-body effects and gravitational redshift inside one sample are now experimental questions, but I admit this is less than B018, which created a classification of phases. So I agree with his structure: if the committee gives weight to a new field over a new instrument, B018 or B010 should be preferred, and I would keep B018 as my first alternative for exactly that reason.

responses.point: Lindroth is cautious about my earlier second choice, atom interferometry (B001), because of the tangled 1991 priority picture and a 1997 laureate in the lineage, and she asks how Zoller would be treated if B010 and B014 both stayed in contention; she also stresses that the Hall connection is a reason to look at the lineage question.
responses.response: I accept her point on B001. I ranked it second at the opening because the measurement physics is what I know best, but credit is spread over simultaneous demonstrations, Chu already holds a 1997 prize, and only a few members ranked it, so I withdraw it as a competitor and I am not carrying it as an alternative. On Zoller, I would not recommend B010 and B014 together because the same name would sit in two parts. B014 is the cleaner pair, Cirac and Zoller, and it is the one I would keep as an alternative; B010 can wait. On the lineage, I agree that the citation must stay on the lattice concept so it is clearly distinct from the comb prize.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B009 first and argues that the statistical payoff of many atoms and low projection noise is the physical reason the lattice works, that the Hall lineage is handled by disclosure, and that B010 is a better alternative than B014 for him.
responses.response: We agree on the physical mechanism, and on the Hall tie being a lineage fact and not a stake. Where I differ on the alternative: B010 has four credited names in the supplied record and members propose three different triples, so there is a live attribution dispute among us that B014 does not have. That is the reason B014 stays ahead of B010 in my list, even though B014 is a theory-only award and the 2012 prize already covers the experimental realisation of ion control. I do not claim this resolves the choice for him; I would only ask that if B010 is advanced the committee settles first whether the third name is Zoller or Esslinger.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks B052 first at the opening but now prefers B009, does not insist on IceCube this year, and says the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and might argue for waiting.
responses.response: I respect that he separates what he values from what he thinks can be defended. On timing, I do not think the redefinition should be a precondition. The work the committee would honour, the lattice invention and its realisation, is complete and reproduced; the redefinition is a decision of the metrology community that follows from it, and the prize would lose nothing if that decision came after. I would change my position only if the clocks' reproducibility were in doubt, which it is not. On B052, I agree that diffuse-flux discovery is established, but the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, relative to AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, is exactly what he calls the weaker part of his own case, and I would want that resolved before treating it as a rival configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the Nobel criterion as requiring a new phenomenon or accepts a metrological invention that extends measurement; this is the question on which my B009 preference is most exposed, and B018 is my answer if the committee reads it strictly.

How much of the attribution to Katori and Ye is defensible against Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, Gill and the PTB and NIST groups; I rely on recollection of the history and have not verified priority dates or the accuracy milestones here.
Whether the redefinition of the second, not yet decided, should be awaited; I think not, but I cannot rule out that others have information on its timing that I do not.
Whether my recollection of the delivered results (millimetre-scale redshift, bounds on constants and dark-matter couplings) is accurate in detail.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. Jun Ye trained in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, where I also spent a research period during my doctoral studies, and I work in the same broad field of atomic physics and laser spectroscopy at Lund. The chair asks whether this requires recusal, abstention or only recording. I regard it as a historical professional connection to Ye's training environment, not a collaboration, a funding tie or a stake in the outcome, and I think recording it is sufficient. I will accept the committee's decision if it prefers that I abstain from the B009 vote, and I note that my preference is shared by the seven other members, so the outcome would not turn on it. My second disclosure is unchanged: B014 (Cirac and Zoller) is adjacent to my own work on quantum memories, which is a reason to treat my support for it as an alternative and not as a lead. I have no documented direct collaboration with Katori or Ye.
